findings.siteText: Cedar Point Design retires a USB drive used for Federal Contract Information. It follows its selected sanitization process and checks the result before considering the drive available for reuse.
findings.problem: "Retires" suggests disposal, but the example ends in reuse. The mixed signal blurs the disposal-versus-reuse distinction that the compliance perspective draws.
findings.guideEvidence: Objectives: "[a] system media containing [FCI] is sanitized or destroyed before disposal; and [b] system media containing [FCI] is sanitized before it is released for reuse." Further discussion: "clean or purge the information, if you want to reuse the device."
findings.suggestedFix: "Cedar Point Design reassigns a USB drive that held Federal Contract Information. It sanitizes the drive with its selected process before making it available for reuse."

findings.siteText: [technical.focus] Verify the result before release. [compliance.reviewQuestions[1]] How is sanitization or destruction checked before disposal, and sanitization checked before release for reuse?
findings.problem: Verification is sound practice from NIST SP 800-88, which the guide cites, but it is not an assessment objective. As written, the imperative and the question read as a stated requirement.
findings.guideEvidence: Objectives: "[a] system media containing CUI is sanitized or destroyed before disposal; and [b] system media containing CUI is sanitized before it is released for reuse." Discussion: "NIST SP 800-88 provides guidance on media sanitization."
findings.suggestedFix: technical.focus: "NIST SP 800-88, which the guide cites, recommends verifying the result before release." reviewQuestions[1]: "How does the organization make sure media is sanitized or destroyed before disposal, and sanitized before release for reuse?"

findings.siteText: Rev 3 adds release out of organizational control as a trigger and names sanitization alone, absorbing 3.7.3.
findings.problem: "Names sanitization alone" can be read as saying Rev 3 no longer allows destruction. Destruction is itself a sanitization technique, even in the Rev 2 discussion, so dropping "or destroy" does not remove it as an option.
findings.guideEvidence: Discussion: "Sanitization techniques, including clearing, purging, cryptographic erase, and destruction, prevent the disclosure of information to unauthorized individuals when such media is released for reuse or disposal." rev3Text: "Sanitize system media that contain CUI prior to disposal, release out of organizational control, or release for reuse."
findings.suggestedFix: "Rev 3 adds release out of organizational control as a trigger and drops 'or destroy' (destruction remains a sanitization technique), absorbing 3.7.3."

findings.siteText: Withdrawn into 03.08.07 (Media Use).
findings.problem: "Withdrawn into" is unidiomatic; Rev 3 says the requirement was incorporated into 03.08.07. This is the same wording issue as IA.L2-3.5.10.
findings.guideEvidence: rev3Text: "Incorporated into 03.08.07."
findings.suggestedFix: "Withdrawn; incorporated into 03.08.07 (Media Use)."

findings.siteText: Identify the cryptographic mechanism or alternative physical safeguard that prevents disclosure; where cryptography protects CUI confidentiality, consider FIPS validation separately.
findings.problem: "Consider FIPS validation separately" reads as optional. The guide says cryptography used for this requirement must meet SC.L2-3.13.11 (FIPS-validated). No perspective on this page says so, and the beginner example's "approved encrypted path" does not fill the gap. A visitor reading only this page could treat non-validated TLS or SFTP as sufficient.
findings.guideEvidence: Further Discussion: "Because the use of cryptography in this requirement is to protect the confidentiality of CUI, the cryptography used must meet the criteria specified in requirement SC.L2-3.13.11. This requirement, SC.L2-3.13.8, requires cryptographic mechanisms be used to prevent the disclosure of CUI in-transit and leverages SC.L2-3.13.11, which specifies that the algorithms used must be FIPS-validated cryptography."
findings.suggestedFix: Identify the cryptographic mechanism or alternative physical safeguard that prevents disclosure. Where cryptography provides that protection, the guide says it must meet SC.L2-3.13.11 (FIPS-validated cryptography), which is assessed under that requirement.

findings.siteText: Keep this architecture question distinct from assigning individual privileges or separating staff duties.
findings.problem: The guide's stated intent for this requirement is partly about accounts and privileges: general users must not be able to perform administration, and administrators perform administration only from their privileged account. Its example relies on a separate admin account and a jump server, and it says logical separation using strong access control methods can satisfy the requirement. Framing this as purely an architecture question separate from privileges can lead readers to discount evidence the guide treats as in scope. (Separating staff duties is indeed a different requirement.)
findings.guideEvidence: Further Discussion: "The intent of this requirement is to ensure: • general users are not permitted to perform system administration functions; and • system administrators only perform system administration functions from their privileged account. This can be accomplished using separation like VLANs or logical separation using strong access control methods." Example: "Policy prevents you from conducting any administration from the computer or system account you use for day-to-day work [a,b]. ... To work with them you use a special unique account to connect to a “jump” server that has access to the systems you routinely administer."
findings.suggestedFix: Review how user and management functionality are identified and physically or logically separated. The guide's stated intent includes keeping administration functions away from general users and having administrators use their privileged accounts for administration; separating staff duties is a different requirement.

findings.siteText: This is not a generic file-sharing rule or media-disposal requirement; the discussion separately excludes deleted-data remnants and covert-channel concerns.
findings.problem: The guide's only example for this requirement credits [a] for configuring the operating system to stop users from accessing other users' folders (alongside patching processor flaws such as Meltdown and Spectre). Calling this "not a generic file-sharing rule" can lead readers to treat cross-user folder isolation as out of scope. The list of exclusions also leaves out the third one the discussion names: components with only single users or roles.
findings.guideEvidence: Example: "You ensure that the computer baselines include software patches to prevent attackers from exploiting flaws in the processor architecture to read data (e.g., the Meltdown and Spectre exploits). You also verify that the computer operating system is configured to prevent users from accessing other users’ folders [a]." Discussion: "This requirement does not address information remnants, which refers to residual representation of data that has been nominally deleted; covert channels (including storage or timing channels) where shared resources are manipulated to violate information flow restrictions; or components within systems for which there are only single users or roles."
findings.suggestedFix: This is not a media-disposal requirement, and the discussion excludes deleted-data remnants, covert channels and components with only a single user or role. The guide's example does count operating-system settings that stop users from reaching other users' folders, along with patches for processor flaws such as Meltdown and Spectre.

findings.siteText: Rev 3 keeps monitoring physical access and adds reviewing access logs at a defined frequency and on defined events.
findings.problem: "Keeps … adds" implies Rev 3 is the Rev 2 requirement plus log reviews. The Rev 3 text no longer says "protect" and no longer names support infrastructure; it monitors physical access to the facility where the system resides, to detect and respond to physical security incidents. Rev 2's objectives [a] and [b] (facility and support infrastructure protected) and the support-infrastructure half of monitoring ([d]) have no counterpart in this Rev 3 text. The change kind (new-odp) is correct.
findings.guideEvidence: Rev 2 (officialRequirement): "Protect and monitor the physical facility and support infrastructure for organizational systems." Objectives: "[a] the physical facility where organizational systems reside is protected; [b] the support infrastructure for organizational systems is protected; ... [d] the support infrastructure for organizational systems is monitored." Rev 3 (rev3Text): "a. Monitor physical access to the facility where the system resides to detect and respond to physical security incidents. b. Review physical access logs [Assignment: organization-defined frequency] and upon occurrence of [Assignment: organization-defined events or potential indications of events]."
findings.suggestedFix: Rev 3 narrows this to monitoring physical access to the facility where the system resides, to detect and respond to physical security incidents, and adds reviewing physical access logs at a defined frequency and on defined events. Protecting the facility and its support infrastructure is not part of this Rev 3 requirement's text.

findings.siteText: Rev 3 keeps monitoring and control at managed interfaces, absorbs 3.13.5’s subnetworks, and adds connecting externally only through managed interfaces.
findings.problem: "Keeps … at managed interfaces" implies Rev 2 already used managed interfaces; Rev 2 says "external boundaries and key internal boundaries". The note also doesn't say that "protect" is gone: Rev 2 requires monitor, control and protect, while Rev 3 a. says only monitor and control. The change kind (changed) is correct.
findings.guideEvidence: Rev 2 (officialRequirement): "Monitor, control, and protect communications (i.e., information transmitted or received by organizational systems) at the external boundaries and key internal boundaries of organizational systems." Rev 3 (rev3Text): "a. Monitor and control communications at external managed interfaces to the system and key internal managed interfaces within the system. b. Implement subnetworks for publicly accessible system components ... c. Connect to external systems only through managed interfaces that consist of boundary protection devices arranged in accordance with an organizational security architecture."
findings.suggestedFix: Rev 3 monitors and controls communications at external and key internal managed interfaces (Rev 2 said boundaries, and "protect" is no longer in this sentence), absorbs 3.13.5’s public-subnetwork separation, and adds connecting to external systems only through managed interfaces arranged under an organizational security architecture.

findings.siteText: Control and monitor voice calls carried over Internet Protocol (IP) networks, commonly called VoIP.
findings.problem: The requirement is to control and monitor the use of VoIP technologies. Restating it as monitoring "voice calls" can be read as monitoring call content, which the guide does not describe. The guide's monitoring looks for unapproved VoIP technologies and unauthorized or insecure use. Its example also covers more than calls: voicemail passwords, phone-system administration and logging. The technical and compliance perspectives use the correct framing.
findings.guideEvidence: Requirement: "Control and monitor the use of Voice over Internet Protocol (VoIP) technologies." Further Discussion: "Monitoring should include the users’ activity for anything other than what is permitted and authorized and detection of insecure or unauthorized use of the VoIP technology." Assessment consideration: "Is monitoring for unapproved VoIP technologies or unapproved use of the allowed VoIP solutions employed [b]?"
findings.suggestedFix: Control and monitor the use of Voice over Internet Protocol (VoIP) technology, meaning phone service carried over IP networks: who may use it, how it is configured, and whether unapproved VoIP tools or unauthorized uses appear.

findings.siteText: Keep visitors accompanied and their activity monitored, retain records of physical access, and know who holds access devices such as keys and badges.
findings.problem: The requirement says to control and manage physical access devices (objectives [d] identified, [e] controlled, [f] managed). The meaning reduces this to knowing who holds them, and implies devices are only things people carry. The guide's definition also includes locks, combinations and card readers. The example partly covers management by recovering or disabling a card.
findings.guideEvidence: Objectives: "[d] physical access devices are identified; [e] physical access devices are controlled; and [f] physical access devices are managed." Discussion: "Physical access devices include keys, locks, combinations, and card readers." Assessment consideration: "Are physical access devices managed (e.g., revoking key card access when necessary, changing locks as needed, maintaining access control devices and systems) [f]?"
findings.suggestedFix: Keep visitors accompanied and their activity monitored, retain records of physical access, and identify, control and manage physical access devices such as keys, badges, locks and combinations, for example by knowing who holds them, recovering or disabling them, and changing locks when needed.

findings.siteText: Prevent one user or process from receiving another's information unintentionally through reused shared system resources.
findings.problem: The requirement covers "unauthorized and unintended" transfer. "Unintentionally" alone leaves out deliberate unauthorized access, which is what the guide's example addresses: attackers exploiting processor flaws. The technical and compliance perspectives on this page include "unauthorized".
findings.guideEvidence: Requirement: "Prevent unauthorized and unintended information transfer via shared system resources." Example: "You ensure that the computer baselines include software patches to prevent attackers from exploiting flaws in the processor architecture to read data (e.g., the Meltdown and Spectre exploits)."
findings.suggestedFix: Prevent information from passing between users or processes through reused shared system resources, whether by accident or through unauthorized access.

findings.siteText: The guide discusses disabling split-tunnel settings, preventing users from readily changing them, and detecting or prohibiting connections that permit the prohibited behavior. / Review question: "How are prohibited settings or connection behavior detected or blocked?"
findings.problem: The guide describes detection followed by prohibiting the connection, not detection as an alternative to prohibiting. Detection alone does not "prevent" split tunneling, yet the "or" in both places attributes that alternative to the guide. The technical example ("reject devices with disallowed settings") is correct.
findings.guideEvidence: Discussion: "This requirement is implemented in the system by the detection of split tunneling (or of configuration settings that allow split tunneling) in the remote device, and by prohibiting the connection if the remote device is using split tunneling."
findings.suggestedFix: Focus: "...preventing users from readily changing them, and detecting split tunneling (or settings that allow it) and refusing the connection when it is present." Review question: "How are prohibited settings or connection behavior detected and blocked?"

findings.siteText: The guide discusses cryptographic and other protections; where cryptography protects CUI confidentiality, the separate FIPS-validation requirement is relevant.
findings.problem: "Is relevant" is softer than the guide, which says cryptography used here must meet SC.L2-3.13.11. Align this wording with whatever fix is chosen for SC.L2-3.13.8.
findings.guideEvidence: Further Discussion: "Because the use of cryptography in this requirement is to protect the confidentiality of CUI, the cryptography used must meet the criteria specified in requirement SC.L2-3.13.11." and "This requirement, SC.L2-3.13.16, also leverages SC.L2-3.13.11, which specifies that the algorithms used must be FIPS-validated cryptography."
findings.suggestedFix: The guide discusses cryptographic and other protections; where cryptography is used to protect CUI confidentiality, the guide says it must meet SC.L2-3.13.11 (FIPS-validated cryptography).

findings.siteText: Clause map: "Employ" → [a]; "physical isolation techniques" → [ODP2]; "logical isolation techniques" → [ODP3]
findings.problem: [ODP1] (selecting physical, logical or both) isn't mapped to any span, although the clause "physical isolation techniques or logical isolation techniques or both" produces it. The other three mappings are correct.
findings.guideEvidence: Objectives: "[ODP1] One or more of the following is/are selected: physical isolation techniques; logical isolation techniques; [ODP2] Physical isolation techniques are defined (if selected); [ODP3] Logical isolation techniques are defined (if selected);"
findings.suggestedFix: Add ODP1 to both technique spans (ODP1+ODP2 and ODP1+ODP3), or add a span on "or both" mapped to ODP1.

findings.siteText: The assessment-guide and model wording remain separately attributable where they differ.
findings.problem: Unexplained meta-statement that reads like a maintainer note. For this control the guide's requirement text matches the official requirement on the page, so a reader can't tell what differs or why it matters.
findings.guideEvidence: Guide requirement text, identical to officialRequirement: "Monitor, control, and protect communications (i.e., information transmitted or received by organizational systems) at the external boundaries and key internal boundaries of organizational systems."
findings.suggestedFix: Delete the sentence, or say concretely what differs and where (for example, if it refers to the Level 1 FAR wording "organizational information systems", name it).

findings.siteText: Retain access records for the organization’s defined period; its one-year example is not a universal deadline.
findings.problem: "Its" grammatically refers to "the organization", but the one-year retention comes from the guide's Example 2.
findings.guideEvidence: Further Discussion: "Whatever means you use, you need to retain the access records for the time period that your company has defined." Example 2: "You retain those paper sign-in sheets in a locked filing cabinet for one year."
findings.suggestedFix: Retain access records for the organization’s defined period; the guide's one-year example is not a universal deadline.

findings.siteText: This wording does not mandate encryption as the only possible safeguard; conversely, encryption does not excuse unrestricted authorized-account access.
findings.problem: The second clause is hard to parse; most readers won't decode "unrestricted authorized-account access" on first read. The first clause is accurate.
findings.guideEvidence: First clause supported: "Implementing encryption for CUI is one approach to this requirement, but it is not mandatory." The second clause is a clarity issue only.
findings.suggestedFix: This wording does not mandate encryption as the only possible safeguard; conversely, encrypting storage does not replace limiting which accounts can read the CUI once it is unlocked.

findings.siteText: Recording risk acceptance or opening a ticket does not automatically constitute remediation or make a deficiency acceptable for CMMC.
findings.problem: This implies that documented risk acceptance is not an acceptable outcome under CMMC. The guide says otherwise: a documented, risk-based decision to defer or accept a vulnerability, with continued monitoring and tracking, is part of remediating 'in accordance with risk assessments' [b]. The sentence also calls a vulnerability a 'deficiency', the CA.L2-3.12.2 term for an unmet requirement, which blurs the two. No perspective tells readers that deferring or accepting a vulnerability is legitimate when it is justified and tracked, and the beginner meaning opens with 'Fix vulnerabilities...', so the page as a whole reads as fix-everything.
findings.guideEvidence: Example: "You prioritize that list and note which vulnerabilities should be targeted as soon as possible as well as which vulnerabilities you can safely defer addressing at this time. You document the reasoning behind accepting the risk of the unremediated flaws and note to continue to monitor these vulnerabilities in case you need to revise the decision at a later date [b]." Potential Assessment Considerations: "For any given vulnerability is action taken for remediation, acceptance, avoidance, or transference of the vulnerability risk [b]?" Further Discussion: "Track all vulnerability remediation to ensure completion; also track vulnerabilities that you have determined not to remediate."
findings.suggestedFix: Opening a ticket is not remediation. When the risk assessment supports deferring or accepting a vulnerability, document the reasoning, track the vulnerability, and keep monitoring it; an undocumented or untracked acceptance does not show risk-based remediation.

findings.siteText: Explain why a security solution was chosen, what it is and how its risks were determined.
findings.problem: 'How its risks were determined' reads as the solution's own risks. In the guide, the risk determination [c] is the threat-informed determination of risk to the enterprise components the solution protects, and the SSP links it to the risk-based choice of solution. The beginner example, technical view and compliance view all get this right ('the threat it addresses and the risk determination'; 'relevant threat assumptions and the resulting assessment of risk'; 'connect to the assessed threat'), so the beginner meaning conflicts with them.
findings.guideEvidence: Discussion: "the security plan provides traceability between threat and risk assessments and the risk-based selection of a security solution". Further Discussion: "at Level 3, the SSP must carefully document the link between the assessed threat and the risk-based selection of a security solution for the enhanced security requirements". Example: "your team uses threat intelligence to complete a risk assessment and make a risk determination for all elements of your enterprise." Potential Assessment Considerations: "Has the organization completed a risk assessment and made a risk determinations for enterprise components that need to be protected [c]?"
findings.suggestedFix: Record which security solution was chosen, why it was chosen, and the risk determination behind the choice (the assessed risk the solution is meant to address).

findings.siteText: How does the organization show that selected remediation actions were completed?
findings.problem: The compliance view covers only fixes that were completed; its focus also asks whether corrective actions 'were actually implemented'. It leaves out the vulnerabilities the organization decides not to remediate. The guide says those are tracked too and handled by acceptance, avoidance or transference under [b].
findings.guideEvidence: Further Discussion: "Track all vulnerability remediation to ensure completion; also track vulnerabilities that you have determined not to remediate." Potential Assessment Considerations: "For any given vulnerability is action taken for remediation, acceptance, avoidance, or transference of the vulnerability risk [b]?"
findings.suggestedFix: Add a question: 'How are vulnerabilities the organization decided to defer or accept justified against the risk assessment, tracked, and revisited?'

findings.siteText: Rev 3 names the plan of action and milestones and requires updating it from assessments, audits and continuous monitoring.
findings.problem: The note lists only additions. The Rev 3 text no longer says 'implement': Rev 2 requires plans of action to be developed and implemented, while Rev 3 requires developing a POA&M that documents planned remediation actions, and then updating it. Rev 3 also limits deficiencies to those 'noted during security assessments' and adds 'weaknesses'. Its update sources are 'audits or reviews', not only audits.
findings.guideEvidence: officialRequirement (Rev 2): "Develop and implement plans of action designed to correct deficiencies and reduce or eliminate vulnerabilities in organizational systems." rev3Text: "a. Develop a plan of action and milestones for the system: 1. To document the planned remediation actions to correct weaknesses or deficiencies noted during security assessments and 2. To reduce or eliminate known system vulnerabilities. b. Update the existing plan of action and milestones based on the findings from: 1. Security assessments, 2. Audits or reviews, and 3. Continuous monitoring activities."
findings.suggestedFix: Rev 3 calls it a plan of action and milestones that documents planned remediation of weaknesses or deficiencies found in security assessments and of known vulnerabilities. It must be updated from security assessments, audits or reviews, and continuous monitoring. The Rev 3 text no longer says 'implement'.

findings.siteText: Span 'correct deficiencies and reduce or eliminate vulnerabilities' -> [a]
findings.problem: Objective [a] is about identifying the deficiencies and vulnerabilities. The verbs in this span ('correct', 'reduce or eliminate') state the plan's purpose, which belongs to [b] (a plan developed to correct...) and [c] (a plan implemented to correct...). A reader hovering the span sees only the identification objective.
findings.guideEvidence: "[a] deficiencies and vulnerabilities to be addressed by the plan of action are identified; [b] a plan of action is developed to correct identified deficiencies and reduce or eliminate identified vulnerabilities; and [c] the plan of action is implemented to correct identified deficiencies and reduce or eliminate identified vulnerabilities."
findings.suggestedFix: Split the span into 'deficiencies' -> [a] and 'vulnerabilities' -> [a], or tag the existing span [a, b, c].

findings.siteText: Spans: 'organizational systems' -> [b, d]; 'applications' -> [c, e]; 'periodically' -> [a]. The clause 'when new vulnerabilities affecting those systems and applications are identified' has no span.
findings.problem: The event-trigger clause is the source of objectives [d] and [e], but it is not underlined, so readers can't see which words create the 'scan when new vulnerabilities are identified' objectives. The periodic trigger is mapped, so leaving the event trigger unmapped is inconsistent.
findings.guideEvidence: "[d] vulnerability scans are performed on organizational systems when new vulnerabilities are identified; and [e] vulnerability scans are performed on applications when new vulnerabilities are identified."
findings.suggestedFix: Add the span 'when new vulnerabilities affecting those systems and applications are identified' -> [d, e].

findings.siteText: Spans carry a, b, c, e, f, g and h (for example 'how security requirements are implemented' -> [e]). No span carries [d].
findings.problem: Objective [d] (requirements approved as non-applicable are identified) has no anchor in the clause map. The guide's own example tags the SSP's description of how CUI is handled and protected as [d,e], which makes the implementation clause the natural anchor.
findings.guideEvidence: "[d] the security requirements identified and approved by the designated authority as non-applicable are identified;" Example: "The SSP explains how your organization handles CUI and defines how that data is stored, transmitted, and protected [d,e]."
findings.suggestedFix: Tag 'how security requirements are implemented' -> [d, e].

findings.siteText: Does the plan describe boundaries, environment, implementation, and system relationships?
findings.problem: The compliance view leaves out objective [d] and the 'Identified and Approved Security Requirements' item in the guide's minimum SSP content. Only technical.watchFor mentions designated-authority approval of non-applicable requirements.
findings.guideEvidence: "[d] the security requirements identified and approved by the designated authority as non-applicable are identified;" Further Discussion, minimum SSP content: "Identified and Approved Security Requirements: requirements levied on an information system..." Potential Assessment Considerations: "Are security requirements identified and approved by the designated authority as non-applicable documented [d]?"
findings.suggestedFix: Add a question: 'Which requirements does the plan identify as non-applicable, and where is the designated authority's approval recorded?'

findings.siteText: When the environment changes, the team updates the plan through its defined process.
findings.problem: The example shows only updates triggered by change. Objectives [g] and [h] are about a defined update frequency, and the guide's minimum is at least annually. A beginner could take change-driven updates as enough.
findings.guideEvidence: "[g] the frequency to update the system security plan is defined; and [h] system security plan is updated with the defined frequency." Further Discussion: "Defined Frequency of Updates: at least annually." Example: "you establish a policy that requires a formal review and update of the SSP each year [g,h]."
findings.suggestedFix: The team reviews and updates the plan on its defined schedule, at least annually, and also when the environment changes.

findings.siteText: A product configuration screenshot alone may not show effectiveness; vulnerability scanning is useful but need not cover every safeguard.
findings.problem: 'Need not cover every safeguard' says scanning is not required to cover everything, which is not the intended caution. It can also be misread as permission to narrow scan coverage, which conflicts with RA.L2-3.11.2. The intended point is that a scan does not assess every control, so it cannot replace a control assessment.
findings.guideEvidence: "By assessing the implemented security controls, organizations determine if the security safeguards or countermeasures are in place and operating as intended." / "Organizations can choose to use other types of assessment activities such as vulnerability scanning and system monitoring to maintain the security posture of systems during the system life cycle." (RA.L2-3.11.2 Further Discussion: "All assets that are within the scope of the CMMC assessment must be scanned".)
findings.suggestedFix: A product configuration screenshot alone may not show effectiveness; vulnerability scanning is useful but does not assess every safeguard, so it cannot replace the control assessment.

findings.siteText: Keep the guide/model wording difference visible and distinguish ongoing monitoring from a single periodic assessment.
findings.problem: This reads like an authoring note and does not tell the reader what the difference is. In the packet, the guide's requirement text matches officialRequirement word for word and the model wording is not shown, so a reader cannot act on the sentence. The audit's verify-sources.json does list CA.L2-3.12.3 under model-vs-guide-differs, so a difference exists; the page just doesn't explain it.
findings.guideEvidence: Guide requirement text: "Monitor security controls on an ongoing basis to ensure the continued effectiveness of the controls." (identical to the site's officialRequirement).
findings.suggestedFix: Either say in one plain sentence what differs between the CMMC model statement and the assessment guide, or drop the clause and rely on the page's official-source comparison. Keep: 'Distinguish ongoing monitoring from a single periodic assessment.'

findings.siteText: Penetration testing checks how an attacker could exploit weaknesses in an authorized environment.
findings.problem: 'In an authorized environment' makes the environment the authorized thing, not the test, so the sentence reads as if the attacker exploits an authorized environment. The intended point is that the test runs with authorization under agreed rules of engagement.
findings.guideEvidence: "Penetration testing is a specialized type of assessment conducted on systems or individual system components to identify vulnerabilities that could be exploited by adversaries." / "All parties agree to the specified rules of engagement before the commencement of penetration testing."
findings.suggestedFix: Penetration testing is an authorized test of how an attacker could exploit weaknesses in the system.

findings.siteText: Use it in risk assessment to shape systems, defenses, monitoring, hunting and recovery rather than collecting reports that never change decisions.
findings.problem: This drops 'response' from 'response and recovery activities' (objective [f]). The technical and compliance views include it.
findings.guideEvidence: "[f] Threat intelligence, at a minimum from open or commercial sources, and any DoD-provided sources, are employed as part of a risk assessment to guide and inform response and recovery activities." Example: "To manage the escalation process for identified incidents, handling specific events, and performing recovery actions [f]".
findings.suggestedFix: Use it in risk assessment to shape systems, defenses, monitoring, hunting, response and recovery rather than collecting reports that never change decisions.

findings.siteText: The requirement and further discussion describe inclusion under the specified enhanced protections or purpose-specific segregation, but the guide’s assessment statements [a] and [b] use inconsistent wording. Their interpretation remains unresolved and needs qualified scoping review. The model wording also differs; do not infer an automatic exemption.
findings.problem: Misreports the guide. The further discussion does not refer to the 'specified enhanced' protections. It says specialized assets in Level 3 scope must be assessed against ALL CMMC security requirements or separated into purpose-specific networks. As written, the watchFor tells readers that the requirement and the further discussion agree on enhanced-only coverage. That could lead to under-scoping, and it hides the real wording difference ('specified enhanced security requirements' in the requirement vs 'all CMMC security requirements' in the further discussion). It also conflicts with this page's own compliance focus ('assessment or purpose-specific segregation'). 'The model wording' is never explained, so readers cannot tell which document it means.
findings.guideEvidence: FURTHER DISCUSSION: 'Specialized Assets within the Level 3 CMMC assessment scope must be either assessed against all CMMC security requirements or separated into purpose-specific networks.' Requirement: '...are included in the scope of the specified enhanced security requirements or are segregated in purpose-specific networks.' Objective [b]: 'Systems and system components that are not included in specialized assets including IoT, IIoT, OT, GFE, Restricted Information Systems and test equipment are segregated in purpose-specific networks.'
findings.suggestedFix: The requirement says specialized assets are included in the scope of the specified enhanced security requirements or segregated in purpose-specific networks. The guide's further discussion says assets in Level 3 scope must be assessed against all CMMC security requirements or separated into purpose-specific networks, and assessment objective [b] is worded differently again. Settle scope through qualified scoping review; do not infer an automatic exemption. (Name the document meant by 'the model wording', or drop that sentence.)

findings.siteText: Protect both audit records and the tools that create or manage them from unauthorized reading, changing, and deletion.
findings.problem: Understatement. 'Audit records' is narrower than the requirement's 'audit information', which the guide defines as including audit log settings and audit reports, so a beginner could leave settings or reports unprotected. The technical and compliance perspectives correctly say 'audit information'. 'Reading' also undersells unauthorized 'access' to the tools, which the discussion frames as accessing and executing them.
findings.guideEvidence: DISCUSSION: 'Audit information includes all information (e.g., audit records, audit log settings, and audit reports) needed to successfully audit system activity. ... This requirement focuses on the technical protection of audit information and limits the ability to access and execute audit logging tools to authorized individuals.'
findings.suggestedFix: Protect audit information (records, log settings and reports) and the tools that create or manage it from unauthorized access, changes and deletion.

findings.siteText: Rev 3 adds review and analysis at an organization-defined frequency and reporting findings, keeping correlation across repositories.
findings.problem: Misstates the Rev 2 baseline. 'Keeping correlation across repositories' implies the Rev 2 sentence already required correlating records across repositories. Rev 2 correlates the review, analysis and reporting PROCESSES, and its discussion says the requirement is agnostic about system-level vs organization-level correlation. Rev 3 c newly requires analyzing and correlating the audit RECORDS across different repositories for organization-wide situational awareness. Rev 2 also already covered review, analysis and reporting; what Rev 3 adds is the defined frequency and reporting findings to organizational personnel or roles.
findings.guideEvidence: Rev 2 requirement: 'Correlate audit record review, analysis, and reporting processes for investigation and response to indications of unlawful, unauthorized, suspicious, or unusual activity.' DISCUSSION: 'the requirement is agnostic as to whether this correlation is applied at the system level or at the organization level across all systems.' rev3Text: 'c. Analyze and correlate audit records across different repositories to gain organization-wide situational awareness.'
findings.suggestedFix: Rev 3 sets an organization-defined frequency for reviewing and analyzing audit records and requires reporting findings to organizational personnel or roles. It also moves correlation from the review, analysis and reporting processes to the audit records themselves, across repositories, for organization-wide situational awareness.

findings.siteText: Rev 3 turns awareness into security literacy training at organization-defined intervals and events, including insider threat indicators (absorbing 3.2.3).
findings.problem: Incomplete. The note leaves out two Rev 3 changes: social engineering and social mining are added as training topics, and new part b requires updating the training content at an organization-defined frequency and after defined events. The AT.L2-3.2.2 note does mention content updates, so the two related notes are inconsistent.
findings.guideEvidence: rev3Text: '3. On recognizing and reporting indicators of insider threat, social engineering, and social mining. b. Update security literacy training content [Assignment: organization-defined frequency] and following [Assignment: organization-defined events].'
findings.suggestedFix: Rev 3 turns awareness into security literacy training for system users, given at onboarding, at an organization-defined frequency, and after system changes or defined events. It covers insider threat (absorbing 3.2.3), social engineering and social mining, and requires updating the content on a defined schedule and after defined events.

findings.siteText: Rev 3 drops in a timely manner and instead requires installing security updates within an organization-defined time period of release.
findings.problem: Without quotation marks, 'drops in a timely manner' reads as 'drops something promptly' rather than 'removes the phrase in a timely manner'.
findings.guideEvidence: Rev 2 requirement: 'Identify, report, and correct system flaws in a timely manner.' rev3Text: 'a. Identify, report, and correct system flaws. b. Install security-relevant software and firmware updates within [Assignment: organization-defined time period] of the release of the updates.'
findings.suggestedFix: Rev 3 drops “in a timely manner” and instead requires installing security-relevant software and firmware updates within an organization-defined time period of their release.

findings.siteText: Each group receives feedback on its decisions and supervisors learn where support is needed.
findings.problem: The requirement calls for feedback to the INDIVIDUALS involved in the training and to their supervisors. As worded, the example could suggest that group-level feedback is enough.
findings.guideEvidence: Requirement: '...provide feedback to individuals involved in the training and their supervisors.' Objective [e]: 'Feedback is provided to individuals involved in the training and their supervisors.' Example: 'you notify the individuals, informing them they failed the training and identifying the area(s) of concern [e].'
findings.suggestedFix: Each participant receives feedback on their decisions, and supervisors learn where support is needed.

findings.siteText: Fictional Cedar Point Design learns that a deployed application has a security flaw.
findings.problem: Inconsistent company naming across the batch. All seven SI Level 2 examples (3.14.1 to 3.14.6 open with 'Fictional Cedar Point Design'; 3.14.7 says 'At fictional Cedar Point Design') add a 'Fictional' label. The SI Level 1 and Level 3 examples say 'Cedar Point Design' with no label, and every AT/AU Level 2 example says 'CedarPoint'. A reader moving between pages sees three forms of the same company.
findings.guideEvidence: Not applicable: site naming consistency. The guide's examples use 'you' and 'your company' and name no company.
findings.suggestedFix: Use one company name everywhere and one way of marking it fictional (for example a single site-wide note), and remove the per-example 'Fictional' prefix from SI.L2-3.14.1 through SI.L2-3.14.7.

findings.file: src/data/cmmc-timeline.json (dates phase-2, phase-3, phase-4); src/components/TimelinePage.tsx (page foot)
findings.siteText: “November 10, 2026 · Phase 2 begins — Level 2 (C3PAO) can be a condition of award, or wait for an option period; DoD may ask for Level 3 (DIBCAC).” … Phase 3 (Nov 10, 2027), Phase 4 (Nov 10, 2028) … Foot: “Dates after today are DoD’s stated plan, not a promise; the sources control wherever a line and a source differ. Read on October 15, 2026.”
findings.problem: Outdated. The FAQ that this same page cites (for Rev 3) says DoD has suspended the move to Phase 2 while it reviews the program. The page presents Phase 2 (26 days away), Phase 3 and Phase 4 as DoD's current plan and never mentions the suspension; nothing in the repo does. The page source label also says 'Revision 2.3', while that PDF's revision history shows v2.4 (13 Jul 2026) added the suspension.
findings.sourceEvidence: CMMC FAQ (Office of the DoW CIO, July 2026, FAQsv6.pdf; same file the site pins, SHA-256 b2563aab…), A-A1, PDF p.5 (printed p.1): "The Department began incorporating CMMC assessment requirements in applicable procurements on November 10, 2025, when the revised Defense Federal Acquisition Regulation Supplement clause 252.204-7021 became effective. The DoW has suspended the transition to Phase 2 of the program." D-A1, PDF p.12 (printed p.8): "The first phase of CMMC implementation began on November 10, 2025 and the DoW has suspended implementation in this phase in order to conduct a review of the program." Revision history, PDF p.17: "2.4 7/13/2026 Updated to reflect the suspension of the program in Phase 1 of implementation." Note: the corpus index also lists DFARS class deviations 2026-O0025 (Rev 3) and 2026-O0043 (Part 204, 2026-02-17); they were not available offline to this review and may bear on the phase dates.
findings.suggestedFix: Add a dated entry: “July 13, 2026 — Phase 2 on hold. DoD (now also styled the Department of War) suspended the move to Phase 2 while it reviews the program; Phase 1 rules still apply.” Relabel Phases 2–4 “Originally scheduled (32 CFR 170.3(e))”. New foot: “Phases 2–4 follow the rule’s original schedule, which DoD has paused. Read on October 15, 2026.” Cite FAQ A-A1/D-A1 under Sources, label the FAQ “revision history v2.4, July 13, 2026”, and check the two 2026 class deviations before publishing any phase date.

findings.siteText: “Glossary | Plain-language definitions that also open inline inside any lesson.”
findings.problem: Inaccurate feature claim. Inline definitions appear only on the 15 Level 1 controls and in some practice activities; Level 2 and Level 3 control pages show none.
findings.sourceEvidence: src/data/level-one-terms.ts: getLevelOneTermIds() returns [] for any control not in its Level 1 map, and it is the only source of terms for ExplainTab and RelatedTab (src/components/control/ExplainTab.tsx:38, RelatedTab.tsx:92).
findings.suggestedFix: “54 plain-language definitions, each linked to its official source. Key terms open inline on Level 1 controls and in practice activities.”

findings.siteText: “Government Furnished Equipment, Internet of Things and Industrial IoT devices, Operational Technology, Restricted Information Systems, and Test Equipment. They can handle CUI but are assessed only through their documentation in the inventory and SSP, because fully securing them is often not feasible.”
findings.problem: States the Level 2 treatment as universal. At Level 3, Specialized Assets are assessed against every Level 3 requirement; at Level 1 they are outside the scope entirely. The visible source label ('32 CFR § 170.19') doesn't tell the reader the cited table is Level 2 only.
findings.sourceEvidence: 32 CFR 170.19, Table 3 to §170.19(c)(1) (Level 2), Specialized Assets: "Review the SSP. • Do not assess against other CMMC security requirements." Table 5 to §170.19(d)(1) (Level 3), Specialized Assets: "Limited check against Level 2 and assess against all Level 3 CMMC security requirements. • Intermediary devices are permitted to provide the capability for the specialized asset to meet one or more CMMC security requirements." §170.19(b)(2)(ii) (Level 1): "Specialized Assets are not part of the Level 1 CMMC Assessment Scope and are not assessed against CMMC security requirements."
findings.suggestedFix: “Government Furnished Equipment, IoT and Industrial IoT devices, Operational Technology, Restricted Information Systems and Test Equipment: assets that can handle CUI but can’t be fully secured. At Level 2 they are documented in the asset inventory, SSP and network diagram and not assessed against the requirements. At Level 3 they are assessed against every Level 3 requirement. At Level 1 they are outside the scope.”

findings.siteText: “…and which requirements are met directly, inherited, or not applicable. Assessors use it as the starting point for every assessment.”
findings.problem: Overreach. A Level 1 self-assessment needs no SSP and has no assessor. The 'met directly, inherited, or not applicable' list is not in the cited definition. It also misses the real consequence at Levels 2–3: without a current SSP the assessment can't be completed.
findings.sourceEvidence: CMMC Assessment Guide – Level 1, v2.13 (Sept 2024), AC.L1-b.1.i, PDF p.16 (printed p.12), footnote 4: "It is recommended that an OSA develop a SSP as a best practice at Level 1, however, it is not required in order to obtain a Level 1 self-assessment." 32 CFR 170.4(b): "System Security Plan (SSP) means the formal document that provides an overview of the security requirements for an information system or an information security program and describes the security controls in place or planned for meeting those requirements. The system security plan describes the system components that are included within the system, the environment in which the system operates, how the security requirements are implemented, and the relationships with or connections to other systems". §170.24(c)(2)(i)(B)(5): "The absence of an up to date SSP at the time of the assessment would result in a finding that 'an assessment could not be completed due to incomplete information and noncompliance with 48 CFR 252.204-7012.'"
findings.suggestedFix: “The formal document that describes an information system and how each security requirement is implemented or planned: the components inside it, the environment it runs in, and its connections to other systems. Required at Levels 2 and 3 (CA.L2-3.12.4): without a current SSP an assessment can’t be completed. Recommended, not required, at Level 1.”

findings.siteText: “The dates that matter for CMMC: when the program rule took effect, when the DFARS clause reaches contracts in four phases, how long each status stays current, and what DoD has said about NIST SP 800-171 Revision 3.”
findings.problem: The four phases are set by 32 CFR 170.3(e), not by the DFARS clause, and the rollout is suspended at Phase 1. This is the text search engines and link previews show.
findings.sourceEvidence: 32 CFR 170.3(e): "DoD is utilizing a phased approach for the inclusion of CMMC Program requirements in solicitations and contracts. Implementation of CMMC Program requirements will occur over four (4) phases". CMMC FAQ (Office of the DoW CIO, July 2026, FAQsv6.pdf; same file the site pins, SHA-256 b2563aab…), A-A1: "The DoW has suspended the transition to Phase 2 of the program."
findings.suggestedFix: “Key CMMC dates: when the program rule and the DFARS clause took effect, the four-phase rollout (paused at Phase 1 since July 2026), how long each status stays current, and DoD’s position on NIST SP 800-171 Revision 3.”
findings.assignedTo: Claude Code prompt item 6 (Timeline meta description)

findings.siteText: “The Cybersecurity Maturity Model Certification is how the Department of Defense checks that its contractors protect the information it shares with them.”
findings.problem: Too narrow. FCI and CUI include information a contractor creates for the Government, not only what DoD shares. A reader could conclude self-generated contract data is outside CMMC.
findings.sourceEvidence: DFARS 252.204-7021 (NOV 2025)(a): FCI "means information, not intended for public release, that is provided by or generated for the Government under a contract"; CUI "means information the Government creates or possesses, or information an entity creates or possesses for or on behalf of the Government".
findings.suggestedFix: “…is how the Department of Defense checks that its contractors protect the federal information they receive or create under a contract.”

findings.siteText: “Level 3 adds 24 enhanced requirements and is assessed by the Government. The requirements come from existing standards; what CMMC adds is the assessment, the status recorded in SPRS, and the contract clause that requires it.”
findings.problem: Contradicts itself (the 24 Level 3 requirements are new obligations that CMMC imposes, with DoD-set parameters) and leaves out two of CMMC's biggest additions: the annual affirmation by a senior official and the limits on open items (80% minimum, restricted POA&M, 180-day closeout).
findings.sourceEvidence: 32 CFR 170.5(a): "defense contractors and subcontractors may be required to implement additional safeguards defined in NIST SP 800-172 Feb2021 …, implementing DoD specified parameters to meet CMMC Level 3 security requirements". §170.5(e): "The CMMC Program provides a means of verifying implementation of the security requirements set forth in 48 CFR 52.204-21, NIST SP 800-171 R2, and NIST SP 800-172 Feb2021, as applicable." CMMC 101 brief (Nov 2025), PDF p.6: "Minimum passing score of 80% (88/110) • Restriction of items that can be identified on a POA&M • Maximum 180-day POA&M close-out date • Annual affirmation of continued compliance in SPRS • Flow-down of requirements to subcontractors".
findings.suggestedFix: “Level 1 and 2 requirements already existed in FAR 52.204-21 and DFARS 252.204-7012; Level 3 adds 24 from NIST SP 800-172. What CMMC adds is proof: an assessment, a status recorded in SPRS, a yearly affirmation by a senior official, strict limits on open items, and a contract clause (DFARS 252.204-7021) that makes the status a condition of award.”

Coverage H1: “Every assessment objective.” Coverage lead: “All 468 determination statements from the CMMC Level 1–3 assessment guides…” Coverage note: “459 determinations + 9 organization-defined parameter statements.” App meta: “All 468 CMMC assessment objectives from the Level 1–3 guides…” README: “468 assessment objectives | Every lettered determination statement from the Level 1–3 assessment guides…” Footer link: “Assessment objectives”.

Coverage lead: “All 468 assessment statements from the Level 1–3 guides: 459 lettered determinations and 9 DoD-defined parameters, each quoted with its page and linked to its explanation.” README row: “468 assessment statements | Every lettered determination (459) and DoD-defined parameter (9) from the Level 1–3 guides, searchable and mapped to its explanation.”

findings.siteText: Home/About: “149 controls”. Glossary/About paragraph: “requirements”. CmmcLevels: “15 source references”, “CMMC v2.13 · September 2024 snapshot”. Controls page: “149 references found”, “Content collection: Demo lesson / Controls & sources”, “No matching references.” Coverage: “Open this lesson”, “Read Beginner in the lesson”. ContextTerms: “Terms in this lesson”. Disclaimer: “Reading a lesson”. Glossary meta: “the terms used in CMMC lessons”. Glossary group: “From the lessons”. README: “inside any lesson”.
findings.problem: The same thing is a control, a requirement, a source reference or a lesson depending on the page. 'Source references', 'Demo lesson', 'Content collection', 'snapshot' and 'lesson' are internal names a first-time visitor won't recognise. The official CMMC word is 'security requirement'.
findings.sourceEvidence: 32 CFR 170.4(b): "CMMC Security Requirements means the 15 Level 1 requirements listed in the 48 CFR 52.204-21(b)(1), the 110 Level 2 requirements from NIST SP 800-171 R2 …, and the 24 Level 3 requirements selected from NIST SP 800-172 Feb2021".
findings.suggestedFix: Use “control” in the interface and say once, on About: “CMMC’s official word is security requirement; we call them controls.” Replace: “source references” → “controls”; “references found” → “controls”; “Open this lesson” → “Open this control”; “Read Beginner in the lesson” → “Read the Beginner explanation”; “Terms in this lesson” → “Terms on this page”; “Reading a lesson” → “Reading an explanation”; glossary meta → “Plain-language definitions of 54 CMMC terms, each linked to its source.”; group “From the lessons” → “Everyday security terms”. Rename or hide the “Demo lesson” collection (e.g., “Worked example”).

findings.siteText: “A requirement that was implemented but is temporarily not met because a known fix is available or in progress, such as a validated cryptographic module that lost its validation after a required patch. It must be recorded in the operational plan of action. It is not the same as a requirement that was never implemented.”
findings.problem: 'Temporarily not met' contradicts the scoring rule: a temporary deficiency handled in the operational plan of action is scored MET. Readers could conclude it costs points or needs a POA&M. The rule's roll-out exception is also dropped.
findings.sourceEvidence: 32 CFR 170.24(b)(1)(ii): "Temporary deficiencies that are appropriately addressed in operational plans of action (i.e., include deficiency reviews and show progress towards the implementation of corrections to reduce or eliminate identified vulnerabilities) shall be assessed as MET." §170.4(b): "Temporary deficiency means a condition where remediation of a discovered deficiency is feasible, and a known fix is available or is in process. The deficiency must be documented in an operational plan of action. A temporary deficiency is not based on an 'in progress' initial implementation of a CMMC security requirement but arises after implementation. A temporary deficiency may apply during the initial implementation of a security requirement if, during roll-out, specific issues with a very limited subset of equipment is discovered that must be separately addressed."
findings.suggestedFix: “A fixable problem found after a requirement was implemented, with a known fix available or under way; for example, FIPS-validated cryptography whose required patch is no longer the validated version. It goes in the operational plan of action, and handled there it is still scored MET. It can’t cover a requirement that was never put in place.”

findings.siteText: “A provider counts as an ESP in the CMMC Program only if CUI or Security Protection Data is processed, stored or transmitted on its assets, and an ESP that handles CUI is part of the assessment scope.”
findings.problem: Misleading by omission: an ESP that handles only Security Protection Data is also in scope (assessed as a Security Protection Asset), and a cloud provider holding CUI is not assessed inside your scope; it must meet FedRAMP Moderate or equivalent instead.
findings.sourceEvidence: Table 4 to 32 CFR 170.19(c)(2)(i): CUI with a CSP: "The CSP shall meet the FedRAMP requirements in 48 CFR 252.204-7012"; CUI with a non-CSP ESP: "The services provided by the ESP are in the OSA's assessment scope and shall be assessed as part of the OSA's assessment."; SPD (without CUI): "The services provided by the ESP are in the OSA's assessment scope and shall be assessed as Security Protection Assets." CMMC FAQ (Office of the DoW CIO, July 2026, FAQsv6.pdf; same file the site pins, SHA-256 b2563aab…), E-A4, PDF p.14: "both the MSP and the MSSP qualify as ESPs and will be assessed as part of the Organization Seeking Assessment's assessment scope against applicable security requirements."
findings.suggestedFix: “…A provider counts as an ESP only if CUI or Security Protection Data is processed, stored or transmitted on its assets. A non-cloud ESP’s services are assessed inside your scope (as Security Protection Assets if it handles only SPD). A cloud provider that holds CUI must instead meet FedRAMP Moderate or equivalent.”

findings.siteText: “Assets that could handle CUI but are not meant to, because the organization’s policies, procedures and practices prevent it. … They are documented in the inventory, SSP and network diagram, and an assessor normally only checks that documentation unless something raises a question.”
findings.problem: CRMA is a Level 2 category only; at Level 3 the same assets are CUI Assets and are assessed. 'Prevent it' overstates the rule, which says these assets can handle CUI but aren't intended to.
findings.sourceEvidence: Table 3 to 32 CFR 170.19(c)(1): "Assets that can, but are not intended to, process, store, or transmit CUI because of security policy, procedures, and practices in place • Assets are not required to be physically or logically separated from CUI assets." Assessment: "Review the SSP: • If sufficiently documented, do not assess against other CMMC security requirements, except as noted. • If OSA's risk-based security policies, procedures, and practices documentation or other findings raise questions about these assets, the assessor can conduct a limited check to identify deficiencies." Table 5 to §170.19(d)(1) (Level 3), CUI Assets: "Assets that can, but are not intended to, process, store, or transmit CUI (defined as Contractor Risk Managed Assets …)" — "Limited check against Level 2 and assess against all Level 3 CMMC security requirements."
findings.suggestedFix: “A Level 2 category: assets that can process, store or transmit CUI but aren’t intended to, because of the security policies, procedures and practices in place. They need not be separated from CUI assets. They are documented in the inventory, SSP and network diagram; the assessor reviews that documentation and makes a limited check only if something raises questions. At Level 3 the same assets count as CUI Assets and are assessed.”

findings.siteText: CMMC Assessment Scope: “Scoping is done before an assessment and places every asset into a category that decides how it is treated: CUI assets, Security Protection Assets, Contractor Risk Managed Assets, Specialized Assets, or Out-of-Scope Assets.” Assessment scope: “The systems and other resources included in an assessment. In this Level 1 guide, resources that process, store or transmit Federal Contract Information are in scope. Scope is established for the organization’s environment; the examples in this app do not determine it.”
findings.problem: Two entries for one concept that disagree. The five-category list is Level 2 only (Level 1 is simply FCI in or out; Level 3 has no CRMA category). The Level 1 entry carries internal phrasing ('In this Level 1 guide', 'the examples in this app').
findings.sourceEvidence: 32 CFR 170.4(b): "CMMC Assessment Scope means the set of all assets in the OSA's environment that will be assessed against CMMC security requirements." §170.19(b)(1): "OSA information systems which process, store, or transmit FCI are in scope for CMMC Level 1 and must be self-assessed against applicable CMMC security requirements." Table 5 to §170.19(d)(1) (Level 3) lists only CUI Assets, Security Protection Assets, Specialized Assets and Out-of-Scope Assets. §170.19(e): "The Level 3 CMMC Assessment Scope must be equal to or a subset of the Level 2 CMMC Assessment Scope".
findings.suggestedFix: Merge into one entry (keep 'assessment-scope' as an alias so its ID still resolves): “The set of all assets in an organization’s environment that will be assessed, fixed before the assessment starts. At Level 1 it is the systems that process, store or transmit FCI. At Level 2, assets are sorted into CUI Assets, Security Protection Assets, Contractor Risk Managed Assets, Specialized Assets and Out-of-Scope Assets, each treated differently. A Level 3 scope must equal or sit inside the Level 2 scope.”

findings.siteText: “The result an organization holds after an assessment, recorded in SPRS for each assessed system. … A contract clause treats a Final Level 1 as current for one year and a Final Level 2 for three years, each with an annual affirmation.”
findings.problem: Leaves out Final Level 3 (three years) and every Conditional status (180 days), which the Timeline page lists, so the two pages disagree. A status also exists only when the assessment meets the minimum score; a failed assessment yields none.
findings.sourceEvidence: DFARS 252.204-7021 (NOV 2025)(a) "Current": "(1)(i) Not older than 180 days for Conditional Level 2 (Self) assessments and Conditional Level 2 (…C3PAO) assessments" … "(ii) Not older than 180 days for Conditional Level 3 (…DIBCAC) assessments" … "(2)(i) Not older than 1 year for Final Level 1 (Self)" … "(ii) Not older than 3 years for Final Level 2 (Self) assessments and Final Level 2 (C3PAO) assessments" … "(iii) Not older than 3 years for Final Level 3 (DIBCAC) assessments". 32 CFR 170.4(b): "CMMC Status is the result of meeting or exceeding the minimum required score for the corresponding assessment."
findings.suggestedFix: “The result of meeting at least the minimum score on an assessment, recorded in SPRS for each assessed system and named by level and assessor, such as Final Level 2 (C3PAO). Final means every requirement is met. Conditional means the score reached 80% and the remaining gaps are on an allowed POA&M that must close within 180 days. Under DFARS 252.204-7021 a status stays current for 1 year (Final Level 1), 3 years (Final Level 2 or 3) or 180 days (Conditional), if nothing has changed and the yearly affirmation is current.”

findings.siteText: “An assessment an organization performs on its own system, following the same assessment guide an outside assessor would use. Level 1 is always a self-assessment. Level 2 (Self) is a self-assessment that must be repeated every three years, with results submitted to SPRS and an affirmation each year in between.”
findings.problem: Gives Level 2's three-year cycle but not that Level 1 must be repeated every year, so a reader may treat Level 1 as one-and-done. There is no outside assessor at Level 1. It also misses a common confusion: paying a consultant to help is still a self-assessment.
findings.sourceEvidence: 32 CFR 170.15(a)(1): "the OSA must conduct a Level 1 self-assessment on an annual basis and submit the results in SPRS". CMMC Assessment Guide – Level 1, v2.13 (Sept 2024), PDF p.6 (printed p.2): "Use of a third party to assist is still considered a self-assessment and does not result in a certification." CMMC Assessment Guide – Level 2, v2.13 (Sept 2024), PDF p.11 (printed p.3): "OSAs conducting self-assessments in accordance with 32 CFR § 170.16 are expected to evaluate their compliance with CMMC requirements using the same criteria established in NIST SP 800-171A and this assessment guide and used for third-party assessments."
findings.suggestedFix: “An assessment an organization performs on its own systems and enters in SPRS, using the same NIST SP 800-171A criteria an outside assessor would. Level 1 is always self-assessed and repeated every year. Level 2 (Self) is repeated every three years, with an affirmation each year. Hiring a consultant to help doesn’t make it a certification.”

findings.siteText: “…requires the contractor to hold a current status at that level for every system that handles FCI or CUI…”
findings.problem: Broader than the clause, which covers systems used in performance of the contract and allows a higher level. 'Every system that handles FCI or CUI' reads as every company system.
findings.sourceEvidence: DFARS 252.204-7021 (NOV 2025)(d)(1)(i): "Have and maintain for the duration of the contract a current CMMC status at the following CMMC level, or higher: ____ … for all information systems used in performance of the contract, task order, or delivery order that process, store, or transmit FCI or CUI"; (d)(2): "Only process, store, or transmit FCI or CUI on contractor information systems that have a CMMC status at the CMMC level required in paragraph (d)(1) of this clause, or higher".
findings.suggestedFix: “…requires a current status at that level or higher for every system used on the contract that processes, stores or transmits FCI or CUI, and allows FCI or CUI only on those systems…”

findings.siteText: “Controlled Unclassified Information is defined in 32 CFR 2002.4: information the Government creates or possesses, or that others create or possess for it, that a law, regulation or Government-wide policy requires or permits to be safeguarded. CUI never includes classified information.”
findings.problem: Drops 'or dissemination controls', the half of the definition that distinguishes CUI from FCI, and the exclusion for a company's own information; it now disagrees with the glossary's main CUI entry. The entry duplicates the FCI and CUI entries and files under 'Clauses: 7012, 7019, 7020, 7021' although it is about FAR 52.204-21 and 32 CFR 2002. The CMMC rule points to FAR 4.1901 for FCI, which the entry doesn't mention.
findings.sourceEvidence: CMMC Assessment Guide – Level 2, v2.13 (Sept 2024), PDF p.9 (printed p.1), quoting 32 CFR 2002.4(h): "Information the Government creates or possesses, or that an entity creates or possesses for or on behalf of the Government, that a law, regulation, or Government-wide policy requires or permits an agency to handle using safeguarding or dissemination controls. However, CUI does not include classified information … or information a non-executive branch entity possesses and maintains in its own systems that did not come from, or was not created or possessed by or for, an executive branch agency or an entity acting for an agency." 32 CFR 170.4(b): "Federal Contract Information (FCI) is defined in 48 CFR 4.1901." CMMC FAQ (Office of the DoW CIO, July 2026, FAQsv6.pdf; same file the site pins, SHA-256 b2563aab…), B-A7, PDF p.7: "FCI is defined in Federal Acquisition Regulation clause 52.204-21, and CUI is defined in 32 Code of Federal Regulations Part 2002."
findings.suggestedFix: “…that a law, regulation or Government-wide policy requires or permits an agency to handle using safeguarding or dissemination controls. CUI never includes classified information, or a company’s own information that didn’t come from or for a federal agency.” Name both FCI homes: “FAR 4.1901 and FAR 52.204-21(a).” Better: fold this entry into the FCI and CUI entries and file it under the program group.

findings.file: src/data/glossary.ts (six terms: access-review, account, authorized-user, device, offboarding, process); src/data/sources.ts (projectReadmeSource)

Further official passages for each term are in readmeTermReplacements. src/data/level-one-terms.ts maps account/authorized-user/device/process onto AC.L1-b.1.i, AC.L1-b.1.ii, AC.L1-b.1.iii, IA.L1-b.1.v, IA.L1-b.1.vi, PE.L1-b.1.viii and others.

findings.siteText: Foot: “Teaching definitions, each linked to the text that defines it.” Groups: “The program: statuses, roles, SPRS”, “Scoping: what’s in, what’s out”, “Clauses: 7012, 7019, 7020, 7021”, “From the lessons”. H1: “Words”.

Grouping follows the first citation, so 'Where FCI and CUI are defined' lands under DFARS clauses, and Security Protection Data and Cloud Service Provider land under 'The program' rather than Scoping.
