Add §170.19 to SPD and CSP so they file under Scoping; move 'fci-and-cui-sources' to the program group. Use “Glossary” as the H1 to match the nav.

findings.siteText: CMMC: first source “32 CFR § 170.4”. SPRS: sources §170.4, DFARS 7019, DFARS 7021, with “Contracting officers check SPRS to confirm a contractor has the required status before award.” Enclave: sources “CMMC Level 2 Scoping Guide — Use of Enclaves” (p.13) and §170.4. POA&M: §170.21 “paragraph (a)” for the 180-day closeout.
findings.problem: Wrong or weak section citations. §170.4(b) defines none of CMMC, SPRS or enclave. The contracting-officer check comes from DFARS 204.7503, not the cited clauses. The Scoping Guide page was not available offline to this review, while an on-disk official passage supports the enclave definition. The 180-day closeout is in §170.21(b), not (a).
findings.sourceEvidence: DFARS 252.204-7021(b): "The Cybersecurity Maturity Model Certification (CMMC) is a framework for assessing a contractor's compliance with applicable information security protections (see 32 CFR part 170)." DFARS 204.7503(b) (90 FR 43560, Sept 10, 2025): "Contracting officers shall check SPRS and not award a contract, task order, or delivery order to an offeror that does not have a current CMMC status posted in SPRS at the CMMC level … required by the solicitation, or higher, for each CMMC UID provided by the offeror." 89 FR 83141 (CMMC final rule preamble, Oct 15, 2024): "An enclave may be able to leverage some elements of the enterprise assessment by inheriting some requirements from the enterprise network, but it cannot inherit the enterprise certification. … Within the enclave, the OSA determines which requirements are implemented and which requirements are inherited; all requirements must be MET." 32 CFR 170.21(b): "The closing of a POA&M must be confirmed by a POA&M closeout assessment within 180-days of the Conditional CMMC Status Date."
findings.suggestedFix: CMMC → cite §170.1 and DFARS 252.204-7021(b). SPRS → cite §170.15(a)(1)(i), §170.22(b) and DFARS 204.7503(b). Enclave → replace §170.4 with 89 FR 83141 and §170.19(e). POA&M → cite §170.21(a) and (b).

findings.siteText: “Its companion, SP 800-171A, breaks each requirement into assessment objectives, the determination statements an assessor checks. Every objective must be met for the requirement to count as met.”
findings.problem: The rule says every applicable objective (N/A counts as met). The entry uses 'assessment objective' for single statements, unlike the glossary's own 'Assessment objective' entry. Visitors will run into Revision 3 (May 2024) and the entry doesn't say why CMMC still uses Revision 2.
findings.sourceEvidence: 32 CFR 170.4(b): "Successful implementation of the corresponding CMMC security requirement requires meeting all applicable assessment objectives". §170.24(b)(3): "an assessment objective assessed as N/A is equivalent to the same assessment objective being assessed as MET." CMMC FAQ (Office of the DoW CIO, July 2026, FAQsv6.pdf; same file the site pins, SHA-256 b2563aab…), B-A3, PDF p.6: "Yes, the Department will incorporate Revision 3 with future rulemaking. In the interim, the Department has issued a class deviation to Defense Federal Acquisition Regulation Supplement clause 252.204-7012 to maintain Revision 2 as the standard against which defense industrial base companies will be assessed". NIST SP 800-171r3 cover: "May 2024".
findings.suggestedFix: “NIST SP 800-171 Revision 2 lists the 110 security requirements for protecting CUI in nonfederal systems and is CMMC Level 2. Its companion, SP 800-171A, gives each requirement lettered determination statements; every applicable one must be met (N/A counts as met). NIST published Revision 3 in May 2024, but CMMC assessments stay on Revision 2 until DoD adopts Revision 3 by rulemaking.”

findings.siteText: “A C3PAO must be independent of the organizations it assesses and is itself assessed by DIBCAC before it can operate.”
findings.problem: Neither claim is in the only cited source (§170.4); both come from §170.8–170.9. 'Independent' is a gloss; the rule's concrete test is a three-year bar on assessing former consulting clients.
findings.sourceEvidence: 32 CFR 170.9(b)(6): "Undergo a Level 2 certification assessment meeting all requirements for a Final Level 2 (C3PAO) … (i) The assessment will be conducted by DCMA DIBCAC." §170.8(b)(17)(ii)(G): "Prohibit CMMC Ecosystem members from participating in the Level 2 certification assessment process for an assessment in which they previously served as a consultant to prepare the organization for any CMMC assessment within 3 years."
findings.suggestedFix: “…Its own systems must pass a DIBCAC Level 2 assessment before it is authorized, and its people may not assess an organization they consulted for in the past three years.” Add §170.8 and §170.9 as sources.

findings.siteText: “The affirmation is made when a status is first obtained and then every year, and contracts require it to stay current.”
findings.problem: Also required after every assessment, including a POA&M closeout. §170.22, where the rule sets this out, isn't cited.
findings.sourceEvidence: 32 CFR 170.22(a): "An Affirming Official from each OSA, whether a prime or subcontractor, must affirm the continuing compliance of their respective organizations with the specified security requirement after every assessment, including POA&M closeout, and annually thereafter. Affirmations are entered electronically in SPRS."
findings.suggestedFix: “…The affirmation is entered in SPRS after every assessment (including a POA&M closeout) and every year after; contracts require it to be no more than a year old.” Add §170.22 as a source.

findings.siteText: “A situation where fully meeting a requirement is not feasible and is not expected to become feasible … It needs no plan of action, but it must be documented in the SSP.”
findings.problem: 'Plan of action' is ambiguous next to the POA&M and operational-plan-of-action entries; the rule says no operational plan of action. 'Not expected to become feasible' isn't in the source. The key consequence (scored MET when documented with mitigations) is missing.
findings.sourceEvidence: 32 CFR 170.4(b): "Enduring Exception means a special circumstance or system where remediation and full compliance with CMMC security requirements is not feasible. Examples include systems required to replicate the configuration of 'fielded' systems, medical devices, test equipment, OT, and IoT. No operational plan of action is required but the circumstance must be documented within a system security plan." §170.24(b)(1)(i): "Enduring exceptions when described, along with any mitigations, in the system security plan shall be assessed as MET."
findings.suggestedFix: “A circumstance or system where fully meeting a requirement isn’t feasible, such as a system that must mirror fielded equipment, a medical device, test equipment, OT or IoT. It needs no operational plan of action; described in the SSP with its mitigations, it is scored MET.”

findings.siteText: “If an outside provider handles SPD, that provider is an External Service Provider.”
findings.problem: Turns a necessary condition into a sufficient one: an ESP must also provide IT or cybersecurity services on the organization's behalf. The entry cites only §170.4, so it files under 'The program' instead of Scoping.
findings.sourceEvidence: 32 CFR 170.4(b): "External Service Provider (ESP) means external people, technology, or facilities that an organization utilizes for provision and management of IT and/or cybersecurity services on behalf of the organization. In the CMMC Program, CUI or Security Protection Data (e.g., log data, configuration data), must be processed, stored, or transmitted on the ESP assets to be considered an ESP."
findings.suggestedFix: “…An outside IT or security provider that processes, stores or transmits SPD on its own assets is an External Service Provider, and its services are assessed as Security Protection Assets.” Add §170.19 as a source.

findings.siteText: CSP: “…and that requirement carries into CMMC scoping for CUI.” 7012: “…and use only cloud services that meet FedRAMP Moderate equivalency.”
findings.problem: Vague (CSP) and too broad (7012): the FedRAMP condition applies to a cloud service that stores, processes or transmits CUI/covered defense information; a cloud service holding only Security Protection Data is assessed as a Security Protection Asset instead. 'Covered defense information' appears in both entries but isn't defined in the glossary. The 7012 clause text (May 2024) is listed in the corpus but was not available offline to this review.
findings.sourceEvidence: CMMC FAQ (Office of the DoW CIO, July 2026, FAQsv6.pdf; same file the site pins, SHA-256 b2563aab…), E-A1, PDF p.13: "Per Defense Federal Acquisition Regulation Supplement clause 252.204-7012, if the contractor intends to use a CSP to store, process, or transmit CUI in the performance of a contract, the contractor shall require and ensure that the CSP meets security requirements equivalent to those established by the Government for the FedRAMP Moderate baseline." Table 4 to 32 CFR 170.19(c)(2)(i), SPD (without CUI) with a CSP: "The services provided by the CSP are in the OSA's assessment scope and shall be assessed as Security Protection Assets".
findings.suggestedFix: CSP: “…A cloud service that stores, processes or transmits CUI must be FedRAMP Moderate authorized or meet equivalent requirements (DFARS 252.204-7012); one that holds only Security Protection Data is assessed as a Security Protection Asset.” 7012: “…and require any cloud service that stores, processes or transmits that information to meet FedRAMP Moderate or equivalent.” Add a short 'Covered defense information' entry or gloss it once.

findings.siteText: “The organization’s own running list of temporary deficiencies and vulnerabilities (a missing patch, an interim configuration) and how each will be fixed. It is required by security requirement CA.L2-3.12.2 and is kept continuously.”
findings.problem: The rule calls it a 'formal artifact', not a running list; 'kept continuously' isn't in the source.
findings.sourceEvidence: 32 CFR 170.4(b): "Operational plan of action as used in security requirement CA.L2-3.12.2, means the formal artifact which identifies temporary vulnerabilities and temporary deficiencies (e.g., necessary information system updates, patches, or reconfiguration as threats evolve) in implementation of requirements and documents how they will be mitigated, corrected, or eliminated. The OSA defines the format … An operational plan of action does not identify a timeline for remediation and is not the same as a POA&M".
findings.suggestedFix: “The formal record, in a format the organization chooses, of temporary vulnerabilities and deficiencies (a needed patch, update or reconfiguration) and how each will be fixed. It is the ‘plan of action’ in CA.L2-3.12.2. Unlike a POA&M, it has no deadline and isn’t tied to an assessment.”

findings.siteText: “…CUI excludes classified information and unrelated private information without the government connection described by the rule. These Level 1 examples address Federal Contract Information, a different defined category; Level 1 explanations do not establish that CUI requirements are met.”
findings.problem: 'These Level 1 examples' refers to lesson context that isn't on the Glossary page; the entry is wordy and ends in a hedge.
findings.sourceEvidence: CMMC Assessment Guide – Level 2, v2.13 (Sept 2024), PDF p.9 (printed p.1), quoting 32 CFR 2002.4(h) (see the 'fci-and-cui-sources' finding).
findings.suggestedFix: “Information the Government creates or possesses, or that someone creates or possesses for it, that a law, regulation or Government-wide policy says must be safeguarded or have its sharing controlled. It never includes classified information, or a company’s own information that didn’t come from or for a federal agency. Levels 2 and 3 protect CUI; Level 1 covers FCI.”

findings.siteText: Assessment objective: “…Objectives help break one requirement into specific questions; all applicable objectives matter. findings.sourceEvidence: CMMC Assessment Guide – Level 1, v2.13 (Sept 2024), PDF p.7 (printed p.3): "Assessment Objective: A set of determination statements that, taken together, expresses the desired outcome for the assessment of a security requirement. Successful implementation of the corresponding CMMC security requirement requires meeting all applicable assessment objectives defined in NIST SP 800–171A or NIST SP 800-172A." PDF p.24–25 (AC.L1-b.1.iv): "This requirement addresses systems that are controlled by the organization and accessible to the public, typically without identification or authentication." findings.siteText: Prompt: 'The scheduled export starts successfully using Robin’s credentials. Does Robin’s employee approval settle the process’s authorization?' Correct: 'No. Identify and authorize the user-acting process, then limit its access accordingly.' Scenario: 'The team identifies the process and establishes whether it is authorized to access the system; Robin’s employee approval alone is not the whole picture.' Visual: 'All three need an authorization decision.' / 'Robin and an approved export process can connect.'
findings.problem: The activity says a process needs its own authorization decision, separate from the user it acts for. The guide doesn't say that. It requires processes acting on behalf of authorized users to be identified [b] and access limited to such processes [e], and it says automatic processes should be associated with the user who initiated (authorized) them. So a knowledgeable reader can argue the answer is 'Yes, if the export is identified and tied to Robin, who authorized it.' The 'No' key holds up only because the process still has to be identified, and neither the label nor the feedback makes that point.
findings.guideEvidence: Objectives: '[b] processes acting on behalf of authorized users are identified; ... [e] system access is limited to processes acting on behalf of authorized users'. Further Discussion: 'Automated updates and other automatic processes should be associated with the user who initiated (authorized) the process.' Devices are worded differently: '[c] devices (and other systems) authorized to connect to the system are identified'.
findings.suggestedFix: Prompt: 'Robin’s account is approved. Is that all the team needs to know about the scheduled export?' Correct: 'No. Identify the export and confirm it acts for an authorized user, then limit system access accordingly.' Scenario: 'The team identifies the process and ties it to the authorized user it acts for.'
